body.text: In short:
Sarah Hanson-Young and Mehreen Faruqi are among the top contenders for the Greens leadership after the shock resignation of Larissa Waters.
But David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May could also be in the mix.
What's next?
The Greens are expected to select a new leader today or tomorrow.
The Greens will meet this morning to settle on a new leader following the sudden resignation of Larissa Waters, who took on the job only a little over a year ago.

Senator Waters said she was stepping back due to difficulties managing a chronic kidney disease, leaving the party again in search of a leader after losing Adam Bandt in a shock election upset in 2025.
The party has been recalibrating since that election left just one Greens MP in the lower house.
Senator Waters, well-regarded and well-liked within the party and across the parliament, was chosen to reunite the party after its election drubbing.
Greens sources say whoever is chosen next will face more pressure to "take the leadership and run with it", with a central question being how directly the party takes on a surging One Nation.
While senators Sarah Hanson-Young, Mehreen Faruqi and David Shoebridge are considered the most likely contenders, in a small party room of just 11, the Greens can also turn out unexpected results.
Among them is newer senator Steph Hodgins-May, who is seeking a leadership role, including potentially as deputy.
The small party room means personal relationships can also heavily influence the outcome, often more-so than questions of policy or strategy — though differences of opinion do sometimes emerge.
A recent example is the split on the Senate floor earlier this month when senators Nick McKim, Vanessa Bleyer, and Jordon Steele-John voted against the party over a carbon credits scheme.

While there are processes for a leadership vote if the issue cannot be resolved, the Greens generally prefer to resolve the leadership by consensus in a fluid process that can also involve picks for deputy leadership, though a leadership change does not require a spill of the deputy role, currently held by Senator Faruqi.
Greens senators and the party's lone federal MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown will come together in Sydney over two days for a pre-arranged meeting, with hopes the leadership can be resolved quickly.
The victor will lead a party which has 10 seats in the Senate, where it wields some influence as a voting bloc, as well as Ms Watson-Brown's lower house seat.
Former leader Bob Brown told ABC Afternoon Briefing that he felt "very confident" in whoever is elected, given the calibre of candidates.
"What I can say is it now has a depth of talent for leadership. There are three or four people in there who would make excellent leaders," Mr Brown said.
He said whoever was chosen would be able to "take on" One Nation's Pauline Hanson in a debate on a matter of topics and "wipe the floor with her".
With the party hoping it can find a way to replicate the successes of UK and US counterparts, former MP Max Chandler-Mather said that would require opening the leadership vote to all Greens members.
"People often ask how to recreate the political success and energy of UK Greens leader, Zack Polanski or New York Mayor, Zohran Mamdani," Mr Chandler-Mather wrote in an open letter to the party room.
"The recipe for their success doesn't just lie in their policies, rhetoric or even organising strategy. It lies in the process by which they won their elections.
"In both instances they were elected by direct member elections."
Who are the potential contenders?
So who are the likely contenders for the leadership?

Senator Hanson-Young, from South Australia, and Senator Faruqi, from NSW, both confirmed they would stand for the leadership on Tuesday afternoon, with Tasmanian senator Nick McKim to run on the latter's ticket.
The pair both threw their hats in the ring last year.
Senator Shoebridge, from NSW, ruled himself out of contention last year, but this time said he would not rule himself in or out.
Other dark horses could emerge in the race, like Senator Hodgins-May, who became a senator for Victoria only two years ago, following a career as an environmental lawyer.
Mehreen Faruqi
Senator Faruqi, 63, is the current deputy leader of the Greens — a post she has held since 2022.
She was the first Muslim woman elected to federal parliament in 2018.
Senator Faruqi grew up in Lahore, Pakistan, and is a former engineer and academic.
The senator has previously been considered as a stronger voice of protest for the party, who might take a more hardline stance in negotiations with government.

She has been a vocal critic of the war in Gaza, leading a walkout of Greens colleagues from the Senate in a protest for Palestinians in 2023, and last year holding up a sign at the governor-general's address which read: "Gaza is starving. Words won't feed them. Sanction Israel."
She also yelled out to the prime minister as he left the chamber, calling on him to sanction Israel.
Those actions were deemed "utterly disrespectful" and Senator Faruqi was subsequently banned from taking part in overseas parliamentary delegations.
In 2024, she won a racial discrimination case after One Nation senator Pauline Hanson told her to "piss off back to Pakistan", which Senator Hanson has said she will appeal.
Senator McKim, 61, is currently the Senate whip and will be running as her deputy on a joint ticket.
The former environmental activist, hiking guide, and an advertising executive was co-deputy leader of the Greens alongside Senator Waters between 2020 and 2022.
Announcing their candidacy, the pair said the Greens need to grow to "meet the moment".
"Our politics is unapologetically bold, and we want to lead with hope over hate and people over profit."
Sarah Hanson-Young
Senator Hanson-Young, 44, is the current manager of business in the Senate and the longest-standing federal Green in the mix.
She was elected to the Senate in 2007 at 25 years old — the youngest person elected to parliament at the time.

The South Australian senator has been a successful negotiator for the party in discussions with government, particularly in last year's environmental reform negotiations — and is seen as a more pragmatic option for the party.
Prior to becoming a senator, she worked briefly as a bank teller and then as a campaign manager for Amnesty International for four years.
She made headlines in 2009 after her infant daughter was ejected from the Senate chamber, which prompted the party to call for a change to "archaic" rules.
Announcing her candidacy, Senator Hanson-Young said the party was at a "defining moment".
"People deserve better than the failed policies and weak excuses from the Labor and Liberal parties and the hate peddling from Pauline Hanson's One Nation,"
"I will fight with everything I've got."
Will others nominate for the job?
Another possibility is NSW senator David Shoebridge, 55, who has built a reputation as a sharp politician and an effective operator in Senate estimates.
"I'm not here to rule anything in or anything out in terms of leadership," Senator Shoebridge said at a press conference yesterday.
"I'll tell you one thing we're all united on. We're united on making the Greens the progressive alternative. Not just making Labor better, but replacing Labor."
Senator Shoebridge is a former barrister and was previously a member of the NSW Parliament.

While being in parliament for just two years, Steph Hodgins-May has also been floated as a leadership option, quickly building a profile since entering parliament following former senator Janet Rice's retirement.
Senator Hodgins-May, a former environmental lawyer, has strong credentials on a core issue to the party, and spearheaded the Greens campaign for a tax on gas exports.

With greens parties globally seeking to replicate the success of now-New York mayor Zohran Mamdani's progressive campaign, the young senator has been considered someone who could recapture attention for the party, which has been unable to capitalise on frustration with the major parties since the 2025 election.
